questions.stem: Transaction T1 reads the items {A, B} and T2 writes the items {B, C}. Which items are in both sets?
questions.explain: The intersection keeps only what both sets share. Only B appears in both, so B is where T1 and T2 can conflict.

questions.stem: A schedule is accepted when (its precedence graph has no cycle) AND (every transaction commits). A schedule has no cycle, but one transaction aborts. Is it accepted?
options: Yes, one true part is enough
Yes, as long as the abort is the last step
No, an AND needs both parts to be true
questions.explain: An AND is true only when both sides are true. Here the second part is false, so the whole condition is false.

questions.stem: Which ACID property says that all of a transaction's operations take effect, or none of them do?
questions.explain: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing rule. Isolation is about concurrent transactions, and durability is about surviving a crash.

questions.stem: A precedence graph has the edges T1 → T2, T2 → T3 and T3 → T1. Is the schedule conflict serializable?
options: Yes, every transaction appears in the graph
No, the graph has a cycle
Yes, the serial order is T1, T2, T3
Yes, because the graph has exactly three edges
questions.explain: A schedule is conflict serializable only if its precedence graph has no cycle. T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 is a cycle, so no serial order fits.

questions.stem: How many different serial schedules exist for 3 transactions?
questions.explain: A serial schedule is an ordering of the transactions, and 3 items can be ordered in 3! = 6 ways.
